patterns.usage_note: The general-rule conditional: it states what reliably follows from a condition, which is why proverbs, math and statements of prerequisite live here (急がなければ間に合わない); for step-by-step operating instructions と is the default, while ば foregrounds the condition as a prerequisite rather than the sequence. It hangs on the 仮定形 stem (押す→押せば, 安い→安ければ); nouns and な-adjectives have no 仮定形 of their own, so they use なら(ば) or, in writing, であれば (学生であれば, 静かであれば). Teaching grammars treat a command, request or statement of the speaker's own intention in the main clause as blocked, but the block lifts when the ば-clause is stative or the two clauses have different subjects (安ければ買いたい is fine).

examples.ruby: もう少[すこ]し早[はや]く出[で]れば、最終[さいしゅう]バスに間[ま]に合[あ]う。
examples.english: Leave a little earlier and we'll make the last bus.

examples.ruby: 少[すこ]しずつ練習[れんしゅう]すれば、必[かなら]ず上手[じょうず]になる。
examples.english: Practice a little at a time and you're bound to get good at it.

examples.ruby: 値段[ねだん]が安[やす]ければ、こっちを選[えら]ぶ人[ひと]も多[おお]い。
examples.english: If the price is low, plenty of people go for this one.

patterns.usage_note: Links a supposed condition to the result that follows automatically, so it is the conditional of natural law, habit, route directions and machine behavior, with a non-past main clause stating a standing rule. Because the result is presented as out of anyone's hands, teaching grammars state that a command, request, invitation or statement of intention cannot follow it, which is the sharpest line between と and たら/なら. It takes the plain non-past form, affirmative or negative (降ると／降らないと), and a noun or な-adjective needs だ in front (静かだと). Sibling 0592 is the same と used of a condition actually met, where the past main clause reports what the speaker then found (窓を開けると風が入ってきた).

examples.ruby: 春[はる]が来[く]ると、この土手[どて]は桜[さくら]で埋[う]まる。
examples.english: When spring comes, this embankment is buried in cherry blossoms.

examples.ruby: 湿度[しつど]が高[たか]いと、洗濯物[せんたくもの]がなかなか乾[かわ]かない。
examples.english: When the humidity is high, the laundry just won't dry.

examples.ruby: 部屋[へや]が静[しず]かだと、かえって眠[ねむ]れなくなる。
examples.english: If the room is quiet, I actually end up unable to sleep.

glosses: supposing that; if we say that
patterns.usage_note: Openly flags what follows as a supposition ("let's say that…"), where bare と or ば would present the link as a fact, so it handles everything from realistic planning to pure what-ifs. The main clause is typically the speaker's own judgment, wish or question, which is where it parts company with the more deductive とすると. としたら takes the plain form (a noun needs だ); としましたら is the polite variant, and もし or 仮に often sits at the head of the clause.

examples.ruby: 今[いま]から出[で]かけるとしたら、何時[なんじ]の電車[でんしゃ]になりますか。
examples.english: Supposing we set out now, which train would that put us on?

examples.ruby: この話[はなし]が本当[ほんとう]だとしたら、放[ほう]ってはおけない。
examples.english: If this story turns out to be true, we can't just let it slide.

examples.ruby: 私[わたし]が社長[しゃちょう]だとしたら、真[ま]っ先[さき]に休暇[きゅうか]を増[ふ]やしたい。
examples.english: If I were the boss, the first thing I'd do is give people more time off.

patterns.usage_note: Sets up a supposition the speaker is only entertaining — a plan not yet decided, a figure not yet fixed — and reasons out what would follow. That objectivity makes a wish or intention in the main clause sit badly (〜とすると買いたい is odd where としたら is fine), and it is the reason とすると reads as calculation rather than daydreaming. とすれば is the equally common variant, としますと the polite one, and とすりゃ the casual one; all take the plain form, with だ after a noun. Sibling 0612 is the same string used of a premise already handed to the speaker and taken as fact.

examples.ruby: 日曜[にちよう]に山[やま]へ登[のぼ]るとすると、朝[あさ]四時[よじ]起[お]きだね。
examples.english: If we're going up the mountain on Sunday, that means a four a.m. start.

examples.ruby: 仮[かり]に会場[かいじょう]を変[か]えるとすれば、費用[ひよう]はどうなる。
examples.english: Supposing we did move the venue, what would that do to the cost?

examples.ruby: 新[あたら]しい機械[きかい]を入[い]れるとすると、置[お]き場所[ばしょ]に困[こま]る。
examples.english: If we're bringing in a new machine, then we've got nowhere to put it.

glosses: if it were …, that won't do
patterns.usage_note: The spoken squeeze of では／ては framing a condition the speaker is only supposing, with a main clause that is almost always unwelcome — 困る, だめだ, 間に合わない, 納得しない — so it lands as a warning or a complaint rather than a neutral condition. After a noun or な-adjective the form is じゃ (では), after an い-adjective くては／くちゃ, and after a verb ちゃ／じゃ from the て-form (食べては→食べちゃ, 飲んでは→飲んじゃ). Write では／ては and keep じゃ／ちゃ for speech. Sibling 0622 is the same contraction applied to the situation actually at hand (この雨じゃ), and 0623 is the verb-attaching ては that warns about an action someone performs.

examples.ruby: 集合[しゅうごう]が朝[あさ]六時[ろくじ]じゃ、始発[しはつ]でも間[ま]に合[あ]わない。
examples.english: If the meeting time is six in the morning, even the first train won't get me there.

examples.ruby: そんな条件[じょうけん]じゃ、誰[だれ]も引[ひ]き受[う]けてくれないよ。
examples.english: On terms like that, nobody is going to take the job on.

examples.ruby: スープがこの味[あじ]じゃ、お客[きゃく]さんは戻[もど]ってこないよ。
examples.english: If the soup tastes like this, the customers won't be coming back.
